content:
In response to climate change and rising disaster risks, the Hong Kong Red Cross today (30th) released its "Hong Kong Disaster Risk and Response Capability Map 2026" study, assessing the risks of typhoons, extreme heat and fires faced by various districts in Hong Kong. The report shows that over half of the districts in the territory simultaneously face high risk of two to three types of disasters, with 14.7% of districts at extremely high disaster risk, mainly concentrated in Yuen Long and the North District. In addition, "hot days" are evident in some parts of the New Territories, with 76% of the territory facing extreme heat risk; fire risk is also highly concentrated in Yau Tsim Mong district, which has a dense population and high proportion of low-income families. The Red Cross recommends that all sectors refer to the risk map for future planning, grasp the disaster risks of each district earlier, and incorporate disaster prevention and preparedness projects into development blueprints.

14.7% of districts are at extremely high disaster risk, concentrated in Yuen Long and the North District

The Hong Kong Red Cross commissioned a third-party organisation to conduct a questionnaire survey to understand the public's ability to respond to disasters; it integrated population, public facilities, meteorological and socio-economic data from small planning statistical areas to conduct research from four aspects, including: the distribution of communities affected by climate and disasters; the level of disaster prevention and resilience in each district; trends in threats from extreme heat, fires and typhoons; and the gap between community needs and current support.

The survey found that more than half (52.6%) of districts in the territory simultaneously face the threat of high risk from two to three types of disasters. 14.7% of districts in the territory are at extremely high disaster risk, mainly located in parts of Yuen Long and the North District. Among them, Lau Fau Shan, San Tin and Shap Pat Heung in Yuen Long District ranked among the top five in the "highest overall risk areas"; in terms of typhoon disasters, Lam Tsuen in Tai Po has the highest risk, followed by Tai O, with other higher-risk areas including Lau Fau Shan, San Tin and Shap Pat Heung; San Tin in Yuen Long also ranked second in terms of extreme heat risk.

Yau Tsim Mong has the highest fire risk; only 30% of people have participated in fire drills

Following the Wang Fuk Court fire, the fire risk in Hong Kong has attracted much attention. The report points out that fire risk is highly concentrated, with the five highest-risk areas all located in Yau Tsim Mong, involving factors such as dense population, high proportion of low-income families and a low number of first aid facilities. However, the survey shows that more than 70% of citizens have not participated in any fire drill in the past year. In some extremely high fire-risk areas such as Kowloon City and Sham Shui Po, participation rates were low, at only 23.2% and 29.6% respectively, while Yau Tsim Mong had only 33.3%.

Yu Hoi-si, Head of Institutional Planning and Humanitarian Diplomacy at the Red Cross, said that the low participation rate in drills is a potential risk factor that may increase the likelihood of fires occurring in the area, and recommended prioritising improving residents' participation in drills in individual areas. The organisation will provide home improvement projects, organise disaster prevention training workshops, and help residents establish mutual aid groups to promote connections and support in order to address the fire risk faced by the area.

The report pointed out that fire risk is highly concentrated, with the five highest-risk areas all located in Yau Tsim Mong, involving factors such as dense population and a high proportion of low-income families.

Frequent typhoons in Hong Kong: Shelters far from North District and Yuen Long

In recent years, typhoons have hit Hong Kong frequently. The survey also found that parts of the North District and Yuen Long are far from temporary typhoon shelters. Among them, Pat Heung in Yuen Long, Sha Tau Kok and Shap Wan in the North District are more than 3,000 metres from typhoon shelters, which is 3.5 times and 4.2 times the average distance across the territory. The Hong Kong Red Cross recommends reviewing the coverage, location and facilities of typhoon shelters to enable residents to evacuate in a timely manner before a typhoon arrives and ensure their safety; and to pre-stock supplies in high-risk communities or temporary shelters before severe weather, and provide emergency support and first aid services to high-risk communities during severe weather.

Under extreme weather, residents are also affected by extreme heat. 42% of districts in the territory face high extreme heat risk, and 34% face extremely high extreme heat risk. In 2025, the number of extremely hot days in Hong Kong throughout the year was 53 days, and hot nights numbered 54 days; however, the survey showed that some parts of the New Territories recorded notably high "hot day" figures, with San Tin and Kwu Tung recording a combined 103 "hot days", nearly double the territory-wide figure; other severely affected areas include Lai Tak Tsuen, Choi Hung and Hung Hom, which recorded 73 days, 66 days and 53 days of "hot days" respectively. Kowloon continues to be affected by "hot nights", with Hung Hom recording 54 "hot nights" last year.

Yu Hoi-si pointed out that severe extreme heat is mainly concentrated in the northern New Territories, while some densely populated areas in Kowloon and Hong Kong Island are also at extremely high risk. The organisation will provide cooling supplies, promote heat prevention information, and make good use of community spaces in high-risk areas to set up temporary rest stations for the public to "cool off".

Red Cross recommends strengthening risk management in the northern New Territories

Yu Hoi-si pointed out that for some areas becoming high-risk zones there are "natural factors" at play, but there are also hardware and software reasons. She hopes the government can make good use of data and information to "prescribe the right remedy" to meet the real needs of the public. Chiu Chuen-pang, Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Red Cross, said that understanding disasters is "only the first step" and that responses must be tailored to the different issues in different areas. She hopes the risk map will help all sectors grasp the disaster risks of each district earlier in the initial planning of new communities and incorporate disaster prevention and preparedness projects into development blueprints.

The Hong Kong Red Cross put forward four major recommendations, including: strengthening risk management awareness and disaster prevention planning in the northern New Territories; strengthening district-level heat prevention strategies in response to the distribution of hot days and hot nights; increasing fire drills in high-fire-risk areas to boost public participation; and improving the coverage, facilities and equipment of temporary typhoon shelters.
